alternatives: Rifampicin, naltrexone or sertraline as second-line options for cholestatic pruritus, with specialist advice.
interactions: Cholestyramine with ursodeoxycholic acid and levothyroxine: binds both and reduces their absorption; take them at least 1 hour before or 4 hours after cholestyramine.
Cholestyramine with vitamin D: reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; separate the doses.
Calcium with levothyroxine: reduces levothyroxine absorption; separate by 4 hours.
Lactulose with the current medicines: no clinically relevant interaction.
output.proposed: Lactulose dose increase, and cholestyramine for cholestatic pruritus
output.summary: No interaction prevents lactulose. Cholestyramine must be separated from ursodeoxycholic acid, levothyroxine and vitamin D and adds to constipation. High-dose zinc lowers copper absorption. Avoid sedating antihistamines.
warnings: Cholestyramine is constipating; review the lactulose dose when it is started.
Zinc supplements at high dose reduce copper absorption and can cause copper deficiency.
Sedating antihistamines (hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine) for itch can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy; avoid.
Rifampicin for pruritus is hepatotoxic; use only with liver test monitoring and caution in cirrhosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No electrolyte, renal, glucose or infective precipitant (sodium 136, potassium 4.0, creatinine 0.8, WBC 5.4, CRP 2.1); bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL and INR 1.6 (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 17); zinc 180 µg/dL with copper 68 µg/dL (zinc excess with copper deficiency); ammonia 78 µmol/L supports but does not grade HE.
action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic and infective precipitants; zinc and copper because she has taken high-dose zinc supplements for 4 months.

action_criteria.rationale: Infection is the commonest precipitant of overt HE and can be occult in cirrhosis; this patient is afebrile with a normal white cell count and no focal source, so the screen is recommended rather than required (EASL 2022).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Flags that cholestyramine binds ursodeoxycholic acid, levothyroxine and vitamin D, so doses are spaced, and that it worsens constipation; lactulose is safe; sedating antihistamines for itch are avoided.
action_criteria.label: Check lactulose and a pruritus treatment against the current medicines (ursodeoxycholic acid, levothyroxine, calcium with vitamin D, alendronate, zinc)
action_criteria.rationale: The pruritus treatment (a bile-acid sequestrant) binds ursodeoxycholic acid and levothyroxine and is constipating, which matters in an episode precipitated by constipation.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe opioids or other sedating drugs: they precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Stop the zinc supplements: excess zinc causes copper deficiency; do not start zinc without a documented deficiency.
Do not treat the pruritus with sedating antihistamines (hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine): they can precipitate HE.
Do not use the ammonia level to grade HE or to guide treatment, and do not repeat it to monitor response (ACG 2026 recommendation 5).
required_recommendations: Identify and treat the precipitant: relieve the constipation (one bowel movement every 2-3 days on a low-fiber diet) by increasing lactulose, and confirm adherence.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
After recovery, continue lactulose as secondary prophylaxis; add rifaximin 550 mg twice daily if overt HE recurs despite lactulose (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Stop the over-the-counter zinc and recheck zinc, copper, ceruloplasmin and blood count after cessation; replace copper only if the deficiency persists or cytopenia or neurological signs develop; ask her to discuss any supplement with her hepatology team.

Treat the cholestatic pruritus with cholestyramine 4 g up to four times daily, taken at least 4 hours apart from ursodeoxycholic acid and levothyroxine, adjusting lactulose for its constipating effect (EASL 2017 PBC guideline).
Keep a normal protein intake (1.2-1.5 g/kg per day) with a late-evening snack and adequate fiber; do not restrict protein (EASL 2022).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated PBC cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 17 (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
FDG PET has no role in HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy is reversible with precipitant control and does not require nuclear functional imaging.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), primary biliary cholangitis cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 17), precipitated by constipation; excess zinc from over-the-counter supplements with secondary copper deficiency

differential.key_features: Treated hypothyroidism with TSH 3.8 (normal); does not cause asterixis.
No ascites on examination, afebrile, WBC 5.4 and CRP 2.1; no paracentesis indicated.

Four months of high-dose zinc with zinc 180 and copper 68 µg/dL; the deficiency is mild, sensation is intact and there is no neutropenia; copper deficiency causes cytopenia and myeloneuropathy, not asterixis or encephalopathy.
Subacute decline with INR 1.6 and platelets 116, but no focal deficit or head injury; CT, if obtained, shows no extra-axial collection.
UDCA is well tolerated and does not cause encephalopathy; no sedatives; drug screen negative.
PBC is an established diagnosis; the low serum copper (68) follows zinc excess rather than Wilson disease.
A two-week subacute course with asterixis and diffuse theta slowing indicates a metabolic encephalopathy; reassess cognition after recovery.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh B (9: bilirubin 2.8 2, albumin 2.6 3, INR 1.6 1, no ascites 1, HE grade II 2); MELD-Na 17 (creatinine 0.8, bilirubin 2.8, INR 1.6, sodium 136).
Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection, GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance, constipation, sedatives, dehydration and renal failure.

Zinc deficiency, not excess, is associated with hepatic encephalopathy (zinc is a cofactor of urea-cycle enzymes); excess zinc from supplements causes copper deficiency (anemia, neutropenia, myeloneuropathy), not HE. Zinc is supplemented only for a documented deficiency (EASL 2022).
Over-the-counter supplement use is frequently missed in medication reconciliation in cirrhosis; ask about supplements specifically.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The low copper follows zinc-induced copper malabsorption, not Wilson disease; PBC is an established etiology.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue Wilson disease workup (24-hour urine copper, ceruloplasmin, slit-lamp KF rings).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: UDCA is not encephalopathic; the episode reflects cirrhosis with a constipation precipitant.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute encephalopathy to PBC progression or UDCA-related toxicity.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Excess zinc does not cause hepatic encephalopathy; it causes copper deficiency. The precipitant is constipation; the zinc is stopped for its own harm.
red_herrings.data_point: Serum zinc 180 µg/dL (high) after months of zinc supplements
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the encephalopathy to zinc toxicity and miss the constipation precipitant.

metadata.difficulty_description: Overt HE (grade II) in PBC cirrhosis precipitated by constipation; over-the-counter zinc supplements with zinc excess and secondary copper deficiency as a distractor; no triphasic waves on EEG; medication reconciliation matters

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. L. is a 63-year-old woman with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)-related cirrhosis who presents with a 2-week history of gradually worsening cognitive impairment, personality change, and word-finding difficulty noticed by her husband. He reports she has been more irritable, is repeating conversations, cannot follow a television show she normally enjoys, and has been sleeping 10-12 hours per night with daytime drowsiness. She had one prior grade 1 HE episode one year ago which resolved with lactulose adjustment. Her current lactulose dose had not been adjusted and she has been taking it consistently. She is afebrile with normal vital signs. She denies hematemesis, melena, or abdominal pain. She has no ascites currently. Her PBC has been treated with ursodeoxycholic acid since diagnosis. Review of systems was notable for 3-week history of worsening pruritus and constipation, with one bowel movement every 2-3 days; she has been eating a low-fiber diet to try to reduce pruritus-related discomfort. For the itch she has also been taking over-the-counter zinc supplements for the past 4 months, based on online recommendations.
